chief_complaint: recurrent severe sinus infections and bacterial pneumonias since young adulthood
hpi_details: 31M presenting with history of 5 lobar pneumonias and chronic sinusitis over 4 years. Lab work confirms markedly reduced IgG, IgA, and IgM with impaired vaccine antibody responses.
ideas: He thinks repeated courses of antibiotics have completely ruined his body's natural defenses, or that he may have contracted an immune-destroying virus like HIV.
concerns: He is worried that missing so much work from repeated hospitalizations will cause him to lose his job and health insurance.
expectations: He hopes to be referred to an immunology specialist and started on a daily preventative treatment to stop the infections before they start.

available_results.test: Protective pneumococcal serotype titers after vaccination

clinical_knowledge.topic: Common Variable Immunodeficiency (CVID) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Common Variable Immunodeficiency (CVID) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management is lifelong immunoglobulin replacement therapy (IVIG or SCIG) plus prompt treatment of infections, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: recurrent severe sinus infections and bacterial pneumonias since young adulthood
Key HPI features: 31M presenting with history of 5 lobar pneumonias and chronic sinusitis over 4 years. Lab work confirms markedly reduced IgG, IgA, and IgM with impaired vaccine antibody responses.
Objective/Exam findings: Markedly reduced serum IgG, IgA, and IgM with impaired vaccine (protein and polysaccharide) antibody responses; no other identifiable cause of hypogammaglobulinemia.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Common Variable Immunodeficiency (CVID).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Secondary immunodeficiency (medication, malignancy) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Recurrent pneumonia requiring hospitalization.
management_principles: Start lifelong immunoglobulin replacement therapy (IVIG or SCIG) and treat infections promptly and aggressively
Refer to specialty team and provide comprehensive patient counseling
Assess clinical stability, monitor vital parameters, and perform targeted diagnostic investigations.
Implement targeted therapeutic interventions per evidence-based clinical practice guidelines.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with symptoms of Common Variable Immunodeficiency CVID: recurrent severe sinus infections and bacterial pneumonias since young adulthood. 31M presenting with history of 5 lobar pneumonias and chronic sinusitis over 4 years. Lab work confirms markedly reduced IgG, IgA, and IgM with impaired vaccine antibody responses.
reference_soap.objective: Markedly reduced serum IgG, IgA, and IgM with impaired vaccine antibody responses; no other identifiable cause of hypogammaglobulinemia.
reference_soap.plan: 1. Start lifelong immunoglobulin replacement therapy (IVIG or SCIG). 2. Treat sinopulmonary infections promptly and aggressively; consider prophylactic antibiotics if infections remain frequent despite replacement therapy. 3. Screen for and monitor associated autoimmune and lymphoproliferative complications; avoid live vaccines. 4. Refer to allergy/immunology for ongoing specialist management.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical features and diagnostic criteria of Common Variable Immunodeficiency CVID
Formulate prioritized differential diagnosis for recurrent severe sinus infections and bacterial pneumonias since young adulthood
Select appropriate laboratory and imaging studies for allergy_immunology
Implement evidence-based acute and long-term management strategies

teaching.one_liner: A primary antibody deficiency — low IgG, IgA, and/or IgM with poor vaccine response — presenting as recurrent sinopulmonary bacterial infections, usually diagnosed in adulthood.
differentials: Recurrent infections from anatomic cause (e.g., cystic fibrosis)
red_flags: Unexplained weight loss or chronic diarrhea (may suggest complications)

must_ask.say: How many chest or sinus infections have you had in the past year or two, and did any need hospital treatment?
When did these frequent infections start — childhood, or more recently as an adult?
Do the infections respond normally to antibiotics, or keep coming back quickly?
Have you had ongoing diarrhea, weight loss, or joint problems?
Does anyone in your family have frequent infections or a known immune condition?

history.answer: I came in because I keep getting severe lung infections and sinus trouble. It feels like every time I recover from one, another infection hits me.
This pattern started in my late twenties, about four years ago. It developed gradually, but each pneumonia episode hit suddenly with high fever and heavy cough.
The sinus pressure is right across my cheeks and forehead, and when I get pneumonia it hurts deep in my chest.
The sinus issues feel like constant facial congestion and thick mucus, but the pneumonias have been severe. Every pneumonia knocked me out for weeks and required hospital stays.
I have had five separate bouts of pneumonia over the past four years, and my sinus congestion never really goes away completely. It feels like my immune system is getting worse over time.
Catching a simple head cold immediately turns into a full-blown sinus infection or chest infection. Antibiotics help clear each episode, but the sickness always comes right back a few months later.
Right now I just have my usual sinus fullness and mild postnasal drip. I don't have any shortness of breath or cough today.
No fever today, though I get shaking chills and high fevers whenever I have active pneumonia.
No, I haven't lost any weight and I haven't had drenching night sweats.
No, my digestion has been normal without any chronic diarrhea, bloating, or stomach pain.
No, I don't have swollen joints, skin rashes, or any dry eyes or mouth.
I've been hospitalized five times for bacterial pneumonia confirmed on chest X-rays. My doctor recently ran special blood tests and told me my antibody levels were remarkably low.
Whenever I get sick, a course of antibiotics clears up the lung infection, and saline nasal rinses give some temporary relief for my sinuses. But nothing stops the infections from recurring.
I work indoors in an office with no toxic dust or mold exposures, and I haven't traveled abroad recently or spent time around sick farm animals.
It has been exhausting and scary having to take weeks off work for hospital stays. I feel like I'm constantly living in fear of the next pneumonia.
As a kid and teenager I was completely healthy and rarely got sick. These recurrent infections only started when I was around twenty-seven.
No, I never had asthma, chronic wheezing, or foul-smelling greasy stools growing up.
No, I have never taken steroids, chemotherapy, or any immune-suppressing medications.
I thought maybe taking so many antibiotics over the years wiped out my natural immunity, or worse, that I somehow caught HIV.
I'm terrified that taking all these sick days for chest infections will get me fired and leave me without health insurance.
I'm hoping for a referral to an immune specialist and a prescription for a daily preventative medicine so I can stop ending up in the hospital.
I have high blood pressure and mild high cholesterol, both diagnosed two years ago.
I've never had any surgeries or operations.
I take lisinopril 10 milligrams once a day for my blood pressure. I don't take any regular over-the-counter pills or herbal supplements.
I don't have any known allergies to medications, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used vape products.
I only drink socially, maybe one or two beers on the weekend.
I work full-time as an accountant in an office, and I live in an apartment with my partner.
I am in a monogamous relationship with my female partner for five years and have never had a sexually transmitted infection.
My father has high blood pressure, but no one in my family has had immune system disorders or repeated severe infections.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 128/82 mmHg, heart rate 72 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, body temperature 36.8°C, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Well-developed, alert male in no acute respiratory or physical distress.
Mild tenderness to percussion over both maxillary sinuses without overlying erythema.
Boggy nasal mucosa with mild clear-to-pale discharge; posterior pharynx shows mild cobblestoning without tonsillar enlargement or exudates.
Bilateral tympanic membranes are intact and pearly gray with normal light reflexes.
No palpable cervical, submandibular, or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy.
Symmetric chest expansion with equal tactile fremitus bilaterally and no chest wall tenderness.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally throughout all lung fields without wheezes, crackles, or rhonchi.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2, and no murmurs, gallops, or rubs.
Soft and non-tender throughout all four quadrants without guarding or rigidity.
Liver and spleen are non-palpable with no hepatosplenomegaly or organomegaly.
No rash, petechiae, purpura, or telangiectasias noted.
